brand.title: ESourceAIG (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Baker Landscape SingleOps on-boarding

questions.question: According to the course, what are the three simple habits that crews will learn to practice?
choices: Attach clear job photos to the correct job, leave a short note about the work, and follow the approved timekeeping process
Clean customer records, create bilingual templates, and implement ChatGPT workflows
Take before-and-after photos, send them via WhatsApp, and call the office with updates
Estimate work hours, write detailed reports, and upload files to the cloud
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the course focuses on these three practical, crew-friendly actions that improve record-keeping without changing how the work itself is done.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course emphasizes simple habits for field crews, not backend administrative tasks or the old WhatsApp workflow. Review Slide 1 to see the three specific habits crews will practice.

questions.question: What is the main problem that fragmented data and low adoption are currently causing for Baker Landscape Design?
choices: Photos are too large to store on phones
The business cannot grow without administrative burnout
Crews do not know how to use cameras
Customer addresses are incomplete in the system
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—the course identifies fragmented data and low adoption as the barriers preventing growth without burning out the office team.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The operational barrier described in the course is about how scattered job information creates administrative work, not about technical storage or crew skills. Review Slide 2 for the core problem this training addresses.

questions.question: Why does the course recommend recording work details while they are fresh rather than later?
choices: So the crew can leave the job site faster
Because the best record is made while the details are fresh and memory is clear
To prevent the office from asking follow-up questions
So that photos do not get lost on the phone
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—capturing details in the moment prevents confusion and inaccuracy that comes from guessing or reconstructing information days later.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While the course does address speed and follow-up calls, the core reason for recording details immediately is accuracy and clarity. Fresh details reduce errors and the need to search or call back. See Slide 3.

questions.question: In what order does the course plan to roll out the SingleOps system to crews?
choices: Timekeeping first, then photos, then Spanish notes, then system cleanup
System cleanup, photo adoption, Spanish notes, timekeeping, and full adoption
All five phases at the same time so crews learn everything together
Spanish notes first, then timekeeping, then photos, then system cleanup
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the phased approach reduces anxiety and lets crews master one new habit before adding the next.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course deliberately phases the rollout to avoid overwhelming crews. Review Slide 4 to see why this step-by-step order matters for adoption and field success.

questions.question: What is the crew's main responsibility regarding the system that the office prepares?
choices: Fix customer records and create bilingual templates
Design realistic workflows and implement ChatGPT processes
Choose the correct job before adding information, use the provided template, and speak up when something is wrong
Train all crew members on all five phases of the rollout
questions.feedback_correct: That's the key distinction—the office handles backend work, and crews keep the system accurate by using it correctly and reporting issues.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The office handles system preparation and automation. Crews focus on a smaller but very important set of actions: accuracy and communication. Review Slide 5 to see this responsibility split clearly.

questions.question: Why does the course call moving photos from WhatsApp to SingleOps "the photo win"?
choices: Because it requires crews to buy new phones
Because crews already take photos, so moving them to the correct job is the lowest friction behavioral change
Because it eliminates the need for any written notes
Because it allows the office to take photos instead of crews
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the course builds on a behavior crews already do, making adoption easier and faster than asking them to learn something brand new.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The photo win is about leveraging an existing crew habit. Crews already take photos; the change is where they save them and why. Review Slide 6 to understand this key adoption strategy.

questions.question: According to the course, what should a crew member's short job note answer?
choices: How much the customer was charged and when they will pay
Which crew leader supervised the work and how many hours were estimated
What was completed, what still needs to be done, and whether there were any issues
The customer's phone number and the weather conditions that day
questions.feedback_correct: That's the practical focus—clear notes document what was done, what remains, and any blockers, so the office and next crew have the full picture.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short job notes are about work completion and follow-up, not billing or team details. Review Slide 6 to see the specific information a good note should capture.

questions.question: How does the course address the concern that a crew member might not be fluent in English?
choices: All notes must be written in English only for consistency
Spanish-speaking crew members should skip the note-taking step
Spanish inputs are welcome and will be auto-converted into professional customer-ready English summaries; accuracy matters more than perfect grammar
The office will hire translators to rewrite all crew notes
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the course removes the language barrier and emphasizes that clear job details in Spanish are more valuable than poor English.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course explicitly welcomes bilingual crew input and explains how translation supports rather than penalizes Spanish-speaking workers. Review Slide 7 to see how the system is designed to be inclusive.

questions.question: What does the "champion model" approach mean in the context of SingleOps training and adoption?
choices: Only the best crews in the company get to use SingleOps
Crew leads are identified to reinforce field habits daily and support their teammates at the job site
The crew that records the most photos each week wins a prize
Office managers compete to see who trains crews the fastest
questions.feedback_correct: Right—crew leaders serve as daily reinforcers and peer teachers, which is more effective than one-time training alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The champion model is about using crew leaders as ongoing support and role models on the job, not about competition or elite status. Review Slide 8 to see how peer learning strengthens adoption.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the core difference between the old workflow and the new SingleOps workflow on a typical workday?
choices: Crews no longer take photos; the office takes them instead
The new workflow is faster, but it requires longer training sessions

Before: scattered photos in WhatsApp and hopes someone sees them; After: structured data with the correct job, photos, notes, and flags so the office has what it needs without interrupting the next job
The new workflow uses more manual tracking instead of data-driven records
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the transformation moves from chaotic and reactive communication to organized, complete records that reduce follow-up calls and enable scaling.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The new workflow builds structure and completeness into field work, not speed or additional complexity. Review Slide 9 to see how the before-and-after comparison shows the improvement in data availability and efficiency.

questions.question: How should leaders frame the 90-day efficiency roadmap to crews so expectations are realistic?
choices: The system will be perfectly fast and accurate by day 30
Crews should expect to record 100% of all data correctly immediately
Progress comes gradually as people practice; success looks like more complete photos, clearer notes, fewer follow-up calls, and improved time accuracy—not speed on day one
The roadmap guarantees specific numeric targets that must be hit every week
questions.feedback_correct: That's the right message—realistic, steady improvement over time builds confidence and sustainable adoption.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course frames the 90-day roadmap as illustration of progress, not a guarantee or speed metric. Review Slide 10 to see how to communicate realistic expectations that maintain crew morale and focus on improvement over time.
